t: SPACEON Adapts Spatial Experiences to Each Visitor With LiDAR Sensing and AI

blocks.cap: Photo - CES 2027

blocks.x: Newjak Co., Ltd. was named a 2027 Honoree in Artificial Intelligence at the CES 2027 Innovation Awards.
The winning product is SPACEON, an Autonomous Spatial Intelligence Platform.

Traditional spatial experiences require people to adapt to content. SPACEON reverses that relationship. SPACEON is an AI-powered Autonomous Spatial Intelligence Platform that turns physical spaces into adaptive, intelligent environments with no headsets, wearables or controllers.

Through LiDAR-based full-body sensing and AI perception models, the platform understands users and spatial context in real time. Based on this understanding, SPACEON continuously adapts content, difficulty, roles and interactions throughout each experience.

blocks.cap: Photo - CES 2027

blocks.x: Instead of delivering the same scenario to every visitor, SPACEON creates personalized experiences that evolve with each individual's behavior, and it coordinates groups of users simultaneously within a single shared space.
SPACEON is designed for entertainment, education, exhibitions and retail. It operates as a unified AI platform that runs multiple applications on the same physical infrastructure.

t: PromLabs Moves Content Production Workflows Onto AI With CREUS, From Planning to Archive

blocks.cap: Danny Kang, CEO of PromLabs | Photo - AVING News

blocks.x: PromLabs Inc., led by CEO Danny Kang, was founded in August 2021 and specializes in AI transformation (AX) of content production workflows. Its AI CREATIVE OS, CREUS, links the five stages of conventional production (planning, production, review, approval and archive), so the same staff can produce more content at consistently high quality. After producing more than 500 AI ad campaigns itself, the company concluded that adopting isolated AI tools cannot clear the bottlenecks in production, and it built a dedicated platform that moves the production workflow itself onto AI.

CREUS AI, aimed at B2B customers, uses an AI producer, CREW, to help with every step from organizing the brief to building scene- and cut-level storyboards and choosing the best AI model. Images take 10 times the credits and cost of text, and video takes 1,000 times as much, so CREUS lets users preview scenes in pre-visualization before generating costly video and checks quality with Agentic QA, which cuts unnecessary spending. Its Creative Intelligence Layer also remembers brand and project context, keeping each cut's faces and product colors and shapes consistent. As a result, the company said, production costs fall 60% to 70% compared with conventional shoots, and a process that took four weeks takes three days.

blocks.cap: Photo - PromLabs

blocks.x: CREUS Go serves small business owners who lack production staff. It builds a brand DNA from store information, Smartstore and social media links and automatically generates an annual content calendar. It automates everything from content generation to social media uploads and Meta ad integration, cutting operating costs by up to 88% compared with agency fees and raising content reach by 78%. PromLabs was selected as a smart-store technology supplier for the Small Enterprise and Market Service and secured 20 annual contracts with small businesses. It has also been selected for TIPS, drawn investment from Honest Ventures and the Gyeonggi Center for Creative Economy & Innovation, and holds six registered patents with eight more pending and an IP valuation of KRW 1.3 billion (about USD 981,000).

blocks.cap: Photo - PromLabs

blocks.x: PromLabs has made the United States its first target market. It presented in the agentic AI category at K-AI Tech Week in Silicon Valley and is discussing a promotional content collaboration and a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Lam Family College of Business at San Francisco State University (SFSU). With support from Korea's export voucher program, it is developing English and Japanese versions, and it plans to widen its global partnerships through CES 2027, the Gyeonggi Startup Summit and SLUSH 2026 in Helsinki, Finland. With its own AI influencer, Hari Kang, and a preview of its AI short-drama platform, TRIPLIX, it is also targeting the global market for content that blends K-culture with AI-driven formats.

Since moving into the Gyeonggi Startup Campus in Pangyo in August 2026, PromLabs has drawn on interpretation and translation support from the Gyeonggi Business & Science Accelerator (GBSA) and on Pangyo's IT and content network. It plans to keep adding use cases for its technology, building on collaboration with local companies and exposure from global media interviews.

AVING News met with PromLabs CEO Danny Kang at the Startup Campus in Pangyo Techno Valley to discuss CREUS, the AI CREATIVE OS that moves content production workflows onto AI, why finishing a commercial video takes more than generating one, how CREUS Go automates content and social media for small business owners, and PromLabs' plans for the U.S. market and AI short-form content. Reporter Thomas Laksoe Frederiksen conducted the interview.
Q1. Please introduce yourself and PromLabs.

A1. I'm Danny Kang of PromLabs. We provide tools that help production companies that have always made content the traditional way do AX, or AI transformation, for their workflows. The service we run is called CREUS.
Q2. How does AX work in content production, given how much AI content is already out there?
A2. CREUS is aimed mainly at B2B customers. We also run our own internal team that makes AI content. To solve the problems that team ran into, we built our own platform.
Q3. You have made more than 500 AI campaigns yourselves. What did you learn from that work?

A3. We even built some internal services to improve prompts and used them ourselves. But even with AI, people were still the bottleneck in many places. For every scene, someone entered one prompt, checked one result, and then a person reviewed that result again. We said we had adopted AI, but we weren't getting the performance we expected. So CREUS puts the way a B2B production organization works onto the platform, from planning and generation to review and even client approval.
Q4. Let's say I'm a client and I come to you with an idea for a video. How does it work, from the idea to the final video?

A4. First, anyone can generate what they want with AI today. But finishing a commercial video is a completely different matter. A video has to go through all those earlier steps, including client approval, before it reaches consumers. So we think generation and completion are very different things. If a client comes to us, we can produce the video for them on our platform, or they can use the platform directly. If they use it directly, they enter their idea for the video. Based on that, the platform casts the characters and analyzes the content scene by scene and cut by cut, and it keeps working with the user on the result they want. The user has to approve the plan before moving to the next step. After that, the platform doesn't make one result per prompt. It visualizes all the scenes and cuts at once.
Q5. Why is making content with AI more expensive than people expect?

A5. It comes down to the video stage. If text costs 1, an image costs about 10 and a video costs about 1,000. That's a big difference. Most platforms generate a result each time you enter a prompt, so people keep revising at the video stage to get it good enough for commercial use. Credits are then used up very quickly. So we moved the basis for that judgment to the front. We do a lot of work at the pre-visualization stage to improve cost efficiency.
Q6. Your service works at the brief, storyboard and production stages, and CREW, your AI producer, even reads the brief and checks the plan. What is the idea behind that?

A6. We focus on getting users from planning, to generation, to the final result. Users come to these platforms because they want a final result. Our role is to guide them to that destination as efficiently and quickly as possible.
Q7. What is the difference between CREUS AI and CREUS Go?

A7. CREUS AI, as I said, is our AI content production service for B2B customers. I started offering AI content services in early 2023, and requests for lectures and training came in, and they still do. I had several chances to teach AI content to small business owners. I found that their situations were often less ideal than I expected. One owner told me, "We take a customer every 30 minutes to cut hair. When would we have time to learn AI, make content the way we want, post it to our channels and keep managing it? That's not realistic." Once they are trained, they do very well. But many of the small business owners I met just couldn't spend the time. So I decided to offer a fully automated service where people aren't the bottleneck. That is CREUS Go.

Users give us basic information, such as their Smartstore or Naver Place link, Instagram and website. From that, CREUS Go builds the brand DNA of the business and creates an annual content calendar. Then it delivers content every month by theme. With extra features, users can also automate uploads to social media and connect Meta ads automatically.
Q8. Who are the customers using these services?

A8. For CREUS AI, we mostly serve enterprise customers. First, there are traditional production companies that want to adopt AI. Second, ad agencies. More recently, there are also mid-sized companies and small startups with in-house marketing teams, even small ones. As AI advances, most of the work can be done in-house, and the cost burden is lower, so many companies want to keep that staff in-house. We serve many of them.
CREUS Go was selected as a technology supplier for the government's smart-store program, so through that program we serve many small business owners.

Q9. Your materials say AI production cuts costs by 60 to 70 percent compared with a real shoot and shortens production time from four weeks to three days. Which countries and regions are you looking at beyond Korea?

A9. I recently went on a business trip to the United States. I was lucky to meet San Francisco State University (SFSU) through the K-AI Tech Week program in Silicon Valley. That gave us a chance to work together, and we are now discussing an MOU. One video has already turned out well, and I understand it has been exhibited.

But even in the U.S., views of AI-generated content are not ideal. Opinion kept getting better, but then issues like Hollywood likeness rights and copyright came up, and from what I've heard, perception is getting worse. I actually see that as a big opportunity for a startup in Korea. Even a service that many companies and people know and use today did not start in the U.S. Korea consumes a lot of AI content, while the U.S. market feels stagnant. So our long-term target is the U.S., and that stagnation is an opportunity for us.
Q10. You are also building English and Japanese versions of CREUS. Where does that stand?
A10. We already offer an English version. As for Japan, we plan to take part in exhibitions there, so we are preparing a Japanese version as well.
Q11. Where do you see the main market for CREUS now, and what about the future?

A11. Right now, I see the main market as AI advertising. In the long term, though, I don't think anyone expected AI-generated content to improve this quickly. It keeps moving into commercial fields, and recently it has been actively used in dramas and films too.

I have often heard that companies that own IP are highly valuable and competitive. Building IP and making AI content is also relatively easy for us at PromLabs, so we are very interested in that area. Recently, as an in-house side project, we built an AI short-drama platform called TRIPLIX, and we are previewing it internally.

Q12. The real test of the market's size may be whether users adopt AI-made entertainment. You have your own platform for AI short dramas, and your own AI influencer, Kang Hari. How are you approaching that?

A12. Our service has a feature called Casting Studio, where you can create AI influencers. I have seen many cases where someone creates an AI influencer, uses it for a few pieces of content in a short period and never uses it again. We keep improving features that let brands own a model or IP and keep using it over time.
Q13. Why does owning an AI influencer matter?

A13. I founded the company in August 2021. At that time I worked with real influencers, and I felt the human risk firsthand. In 2022, I came across Stable Diffusion, and the first thing I made with it was an AI influencer. It was sensational then, but looking back, the quality was quite crude. What we called virtual influencers then has fully turned into what we now call AI influencers, and I think that market will grow very quickly.

In China, an AI actor called Pangtaozi is reportedly earning more than 50 million won (about USD 38,000) for a one-minute ad. Inside China, demand for AI dramas and short dramas is very large in the domestic market. That is a plan for the future, but in the long term we expect K-culture and AI content formats to combine and open up a global market.
Q14. What are the benefits of being at the Startup Campus in Pangyo?

A14. We moved to Pangyo this August. The best thing so far is that we have far more chances to build networks and exchange ideas with other companies than before. Not only me, but my team members are also working with various companies in Pangyo.

t: AiRET Cleans Leather and Suede Shoes at Home Without Submerging Them in Water

blocks.cap: Photo - AiRET

blocks.x: Leather and suede shoes are normally sent to a cleaner because they cannot be washed at home.

AiRET Inc, a smart home hardware developer focused on the entryway and led by CEO Bon-Ung Koo, exhibited the AX1 at the 57th Korea Electronics Show (KES 2026), held from Oct. 13 to 16 at COEX in Seoul. The AX1 is a fully automatic household shoe cleaner that does not immerse shoes in water. At the show, AiRET received an Innovation Award in the AI transformation (AX) category, alongside recipients including Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics. The company says it came with two goals: to widen contact with domestic home appliance distribution channels and to identify B2B adopters in hotels and residential developments.

The user places the shoes inside and closes the door, and the whole process from recognition to cleaning runs automatically. Vision AI embedded in the device identifies the type and material of each pair and determines the cleaning conditions on its own, so the user never selects a material setting or adjusts cleaning intensity. Because shoes are not submerged, AiRET says materials such as leather and suede can be handled at home.

At its booth, the company showed a full-scale 1:1 model that revealed the internal structure and the cleaning sequence, and ran continuous docent sessions explaining how the product works and the thinking behind its design. It will reflect the domestic feedback gathered at KES 2026 in its CES exhibit in January 2027.

AiRET started its business in 2024 and incorporated in April 2025. Three of its six employees work in research and development. It has received transfers of four patented technologies from a major Korean corporation and a public institution and applies them in product development. In 2026, it was selected for the NIPA's High-Performance Computing Support Program and received an H100 GPU, which it uses to train its shoe recognition models. It also won a CES 2026 Innovation Award and has confirmed its participation in Eureka Park at CES 2027.

blocks.cap: AiRET exhibit at KES 2026 | Photo - AiRET

blocks.x: The AX1 is in the final stage before mass production, and AiRET has no formal export sales yet. It has signed a proof-of-concept (PoC) agreement for product adoption with a luxury homebuilder based in Las Vegas. In August 2026, it took part in THECA 2026 in Bangkok at the official invitation of the Thailand Board of Investment (BOI), where it identified local distribution and supply chain partners. In Korea, it has been selected for the Korea Institute of Design Promotion's Style (Design) Tech program and the Federation of Korean Entrepreneurs' Plus Startup program.

AiRET's priority markets are North America and Dubai in the United Arab Emirates. In North America, it cites the high proportion of detached housing, which creates demand for shoe care around entryways and garages, and the practice of building appliances into new homes, which makes entry through homebuilders viable. It chose Dubai because the custom of removing shoes indoors gives it a demand structure for entryway products similar to Korea's, because sand and dust from the desert climate make shoe cleaning a constant need, and because active construction of luxury villas and residences, with strong purchasing power for premium appliances, supports the price of an early-entry product. It also sees Dubai as a base for expanding across the GCC region.

The company is looking for local distributors of premium home appliances, homebuilders and interior contractors that install appliances in new housing, and hotel and residence operators able to adopt the product room by room. It gives priority to partners that can handle installation and after-sales service in addition to distribution.

AiRET's immediate goal is to take part in CES in January 2027 and introduce the product formally to the North American market. It is also prioritizing mass production for a domestic launch and converting the PoC agreement with the U.S. homebuilder into actual supply. In Dubai, it aims to find local distribution partners and hotel and residence operators and ship its first export volume during 2027. It plans to offer the freestanding AX1 alongside a built-in model, for general households and new residential construction respectively.

The 57th Korea Electronics Show (KES 2026) ran from Oct. 13 (Tuesday) to 16 (Friday) in Halls A and B at COEX in Seoul. The Korea Electronics Association (KEA) organized the show, and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources hosted it. The KES website lists 500 exhibitors and 1,100 booths. Its themes included electronic parts and materials such as sensors, connectors, printed circuit boards (PCBs) and power supplies; AI transformation (AX) fields such as generative AI, on-device AI, AI chips and smart home and wearable devices; mobility; robotics; digital health; ESG; and Web 3.0 and XR. Alongside the co-located XR & Spatial Computing Show, the event featured X-SPACE 2026, a special exhibition covering digital twins, industrial XR, spatial intelligence, XR devices and spatial computing platforms. The Innovation Awards ceremony took place on Oct. 13.

t: HELIOS Offers Taiwanese Manufacturers Free Eight-Week Supply Chain Risk Pilot

blocks.cap: The 2026 Pangyo Global Media Meet Up Season II takes place at Gyeonggi Startup Campus | Photo - AVING News

blocks.x: HELIOS, a Pangyo startup specializing in supply chain risk intelligence, is offering Taiwanese component makers and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) companies a free eight-week analysis of the suppliers behind one product line. The company proposed the pilot on Oct. 6 at the 2026 Pangyo Global Media Meet Up Season II, where it presented HELIOS ATLAS and HELIOS AEGIS to Taiwan's DIGITIMES.

Gyeonggido Business & Science Accelerator (GBSA) hosted the event at The Link in Gyeonggi Startup Campus to raise the global profile of Pangyo Techno Valley and support overseas media coverage and market entry for Pangyo startups. HELIOS was the featured company, and Yuhyun Kim, CEO of HELIOS, outlined its strategy for Taiwan and global supply chain markets.

HELIOS was founded in June 2023 on experience in overseas field research and a simple principle: deliver verified information rather than collect more of it. Its systems gather multilingual news, public disclosures, ship and aircraft tracking data, satellite-detected hot spots and commodity prices, then cross-check them. In-house analysts and a local network across Asia review the results, and customers receive only risk information that has been confirmed, along with the evidence behind it.

blocks.cap: HELIOS ATLAS and HELIOS AEGIS | Photo - HELIOS

blocks.x: HELIOS ATLAS is a business-to-business service that overlays external risk information on a manufacturer's or exporter's supplier list. It continuously monitors suppliers at the third tier and below for sanctions involvement, dependence on a single country, opaque beneficial ownership, counterfeit parts and signs of supply disruption. HELIOS AEGIS runs the same analysis engine on a closed network isolated from external networks. It provides security briefings and strategic-materials supply alerts to defense and public agencies.The company points to two design choices. It treats an event as confirmed only when two or more independent signals agree, which it says sharply reduces false alarms. And because AEGIS runs on a closed network, data does not leave for overseas cloud services.

HELIOS has set up a U.S. entity, HELIOS Security Solutions LLC, to pursue defense and supply chain markets. It has named Taiwan as its second major target. Like Korea, Taiwan is a core hub of the global semiconductor and AI supply chain, and HELIOS sees strong demand there tied to compliance with Section 805 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 (NDAA). The free pilot for Taiwanese parts makers and EMS companies is meant to open the door to local partnerships.

Two milestones are planned. HELIOS will file a core patent under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) in December 2026, and it will exhibit at CES 2027 in January in Gyeonggi Province's pavilion at Eureka Park.

Kim said HELIOS is based at Gyeonggi Startup Bridge in 2nd Pangyo Techno Valley, where it works with AI, semiconductor and software companies and uses GBSA's global support programs. After the DIGITIMES presentation, he said, the company aims to become an essential partner in managing sub-supplier risk for Korean and Taiwanese companies that supply global defense and IT supply chains.

blocks.cap: (From left) Seungyu Kang of DIGITIMES and Yuhyun Kim, CEO of HELIOS | Photo - AVING News

blocks.x: Founded in 1998, DIGITIMES is Taiwan's largest technology media outlet. It runs Traditional Chinese and English editions and provides analysis on semiconductors, electronics, telecommunications and the ICT supply chain to technology companies and investors around the world.

Pangyo Techno Valley brings together Research (R), People (P), Information (I) and Trade (T) as a global convergence R&D hub built around IT, BT, CT and NT. Gyeonggi Province developed it as an innovation cluster to secure new growth engines for the country through technology innovation, workforce training, job creation and stronger international business competitiveness. t: upfall Presents Soul by voidX, an Emotion-Aware AI Agent That Speaks in a Brand's Own Voice

blocks.cap: Photo - upfall

blocks.x: Nautilus Investment is running a global corporate collaboration program in New York from Oct. 13 to Oct. 18, 2026, to support Korean companies entering the U.S. market. The program includes a cross-border forum and investor relations (IR) sessions, local workshops, the Small Business Expo, KOOM Stage, KOOM Haus and networking events. Participating companies will present their technologies and products to buyers, investors and other stakeholders in New York while exploring opportunities for partnerships, investment and market entry. Nautilus Investment, a U.S.-affiliated venture capital firm based in Songdo, Incheon, was founded in 2019 and also operates global corporate collaboration programs connecting startups with technology companies such as NVIDIA, Microsoft and ANSYS.
A shopper who asks a brand's chatbot a question often gets a correct answer that sounds like it came from nowhere, with no sense of the brand behind it and no memory of the last visit.
Giving the agent the brand's knowledge, personality and a record of the relationship is the idea behind upfall's work.

upfall Co., Ltd., founded in 2022 and led by co-CEOs Soyoung Lee and Yerim Lee, develops emotion-aware AI agents. Its brand-dedicated service, Soul by voidX, connects a brand's products, policies and content with customer interests, with e-commerce as the initial core market. It supports the shopper from product discovery and inquiries to recommendations and return visits.

Three technologies underpin it. An ontology organizes brand information and customer needs into a relationship graph, emotion inference estimates emotional changes from the conversation, and RQ (Relationship Quotient), upfall's proprietary metric, tracks the depth of the relationship across interactions. Using information customers share with consent, Soul is designed to carry context into later conversations. It keeps to the brand's facts and commitments while adapting how it speaks to each customer's situation.

Soul reads product information, brand stories and policies from a brand's website URL and configures an agent that reflects the brand's personality and tone of voice. It has three roles. The In-house Agent manages brand knowledge and tracks brand visibility in AI-generated answers. The Customer Agent talks with visitors on the brand's site and guides them through products and content. The Ad Agent discloses that it is advertising and starts on-site conversations only within the scope of user consent. Brand news, content and events are woven into the conversation, giving shoppers a reason to engage with a brand beyond a purchase.

The company says it has carried out at least 50 AI projects across five industries over four years. In an in-house AI agent proof of concept for a major Korean company, its own measurements showed response time for complex knowledge queries falling from six minutes to 50 seconds. It built an AI learning agent based on educational content for the Korea Management Association and runs agents for inquiries and appointment booking at five medical institutions. upfall was selected for NVIDIA N&up 2026, signed an MOU with Alibaba Cloud in 2024, and was chosen by the Seoul Metropolitan Government to take part in Eureka Park at CES 2027, where it is preparing a Soul demo and 3D character agents.

The United States and Japan are its main target markets. In the United States, upfall is working to secure its first paid contract with an e-commerce brand, and in Japan it is exploring follow-on opportunities based on its semiconductor process simulation experience. It is looking for local brands that want to improve customer experience, e-commerce platform builders and operators, and businesses able to run joint pilots.

upfall plans to combine monthly subscriptions with customized enterprise deployments and to compare purchase conversion, return visits and repeat purchases between groups with and without the agent in controlled tests. The results will inform product improvements and the business model, and performance-linked fees remain under consideration pending the validation results. Over the longer term, it plans to extend its emotion inference, memory and relationship management into entertainment and other industries through 3D character agents that express conversational context through facial expressions, voice and reactions. Buyer matching, overseas pilot funding and multilingual localization are the support it wants most.

t: PLASBIO Shows Physical AI Microinjection Robot for Preclinical Research at KES 2026 (Innovation Awards Winner)

blocks.cap: Photo - PLASBIO

blocks.x: Tail vein injections and head fixation in animal studies have long relied on the hands of skilled researchers, so results can vary with who performs the procedure.
PLASBIO has taken the route of handing those steps to a vision AI-guided robot, with the aim of making every run repeatable.

PLASBIO Inc., a preclinical research automation company founded in November 2020 and led by CEO Sunggurl Park, builds laboratory automation equipment and AI solutions around that approach. The company is headquartered in Jeonju, Jeonbuk, with a branch in Daejeon, and its goal is to automate biomedical research and standardize the experimental data produced in the preclinical stage.

PLASBIO's main products are the Smart Inject and Brain Inject series, which automate and digitize microinjections and precision experiments on small animals. At the core are on-device automation algorithms that combine AI-based image and motion recognition with precision robotics control. The company automates tail vein injection and stereotaxic head fixation, tasks that previously depended solely on the manual skill of experts, which it says reduces errors tied to researcher skill and improves reproducibility and data reliability. Vision AI detects the condition of the animal in real time and works with the robot.

At KES 2026, PLASBIO is showing its Physical AI-based Microinjection Robot System, an upgraded Smart Inject product, together with a Real-Time Integrated Monitoring Solution that pairs AI-based control software with an intuitive interface. The system automates the microinjection of research models such as cells, embryos and organoids in one all-in-one unit.

The company points to two differentiators. The first is an integrated all-in-one layout that combines the anti-vibration table, robotic arm, display and wiring, previously separate, in a single housing. The second is a vibration reduction design built around a decoupled base, vibration pads and cable management components, which the company says cuts vibration from the 6-axis robotic arm by more than 30%. An adjustable display mount and an AI-based interface complete the design.

PLASBIO is using the show to check the product's technology and design in the global market ahead of its official exhibition at CES 2027. It is also looking for partnerships and new buyers among biopharmaceutical companies, non-clinical contract research organizations (CROs) and research equipment distributors in North America and Europe.

In Korea, PLASBIO supplies its solutions to KAIST, the Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology (KRIBB), the Korea Institute of Toxicology (KIT), Kangwon National University and Chonbuk National University Hospital. The company recorded revenue of KRW 2.1 billion (about USD 1.5 million) in 2025 and aims for KRW 4.6 billion in 2026 by supplying Innovative Procurement Products and expanding deliveries to major institutions.

Overseas, PLASBIO has completed US patent registrations and takes part in NVIDIA Inception and Microsoft's startup support program. It is conducting joint research with Harvard Medical School and the Johns Hopkins Institute for NanoBioTechnology (INBT), is a member of the Chicago-based healthcare innovation institution MATTER and the hard-tech innovation institution mHUB, and was selected in 2026 for the Ministry of Health and Welfare's Research-Driven Hospital Harvard International Cooperation Project. It also took part in the BIO International Convention in 2025 and 2026.

The company's target regions are North America, Europe and Japan. It wants to work with global research equipment distributors that have direct networks with local research institutes and pharmaceutical companies and can provide installation and technical support, and with global non-clinical CROs and large biopharmaceutical companies that would adopt its robots in drug evaluation and help build reference cases. PLASBIO plans to show a new Smart Inject model at CES 2027 and the BIO International Convention 2027, and to raise the share of subscription-based AI data and software revenue as hardware deployments grow. Overseas FDA, CE and ISO certification, which takes time and money, is its main obstacle.

KES 2026, the 57th Korea Electronics Show, runs Oct. 13 to Oct. 16 at COEX Halls A and B in Seoul. t: MeTown Brings 3D Crime Scene Reconstruction Built From Phone Photos to KPEX 2026

blocks.cap: Photo - MeTown

blocks.x: Documenting a crime scene in 3D usually takes a specialized scanner and an outside production team. The result is expensive, slow to produce, and something investigators can only look at.

MeTown Inc., an AI neural rendering company in Seoul, says it can do it with a phone. Led by CEO Dohae Lee, the company will take part in Korea Police World Expo 2026 (KPEX 2026), where it will present EVOVA Forensics, a forensic platform that rebuilds a scene in 3D from mobile photographs and on-site investigation data.

MeTown was established in March 2023 as a joint venture with Yonsei University Technology Holdings. It says it is headquartered in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, with a studio and branch in Mapo-gu, Seoul, and that most of its 13 employees are graduate-level researchers in AI and computer graphics. Its core technology is the Spatial Cognition Engine, which extends its VFGS (View Flexible Gaussian Splatting) neural rendering technology, a winner of a CES 2025 Innovation Award, to entire spaces. The company says it reconstructs real spaces in precise 3D from photographs or video alone, with natural-language AI interaction for measurement, analysis and search inside the reconstructed scene. It says the system runs on standard PCs without specialized scanners or outsourced 3D production, with data under 3 megabytes and rendering above 100 frames per second.

According to MeTown, EVOVA Forensics reconstructs most crime scenes from a single camera walk-through and then supports measurement, anomaly detection, temporal change detection and cross-case similarity search within the space, all through conversation and without 3D software training. As an example, the company says that when an investigator asks for the distance between a door and a window, the system answers with evidence-backed measurements, and that even a finding of no evidence is delivered as a falsifiable conclusion with quantitative justification. The platform also includes a bloodstain pattern analysis function, which the company says is the same type of analysis that played a decisive role in solving the Itaewon murder case.

On its record, MeTown says it has delivered more than 4,000 paid 3D data items since launching its EVOVA 3D ShowRoom service for e-commerce in May 2024. Its Korean clients include The North Face, FCMM, Samsung C&T Fashion, Mind Bridge and Home&Shopping, and it says The North Face adopted the showroom across its online store, with about 99% cost savings and an 84% reduction in production time. In public safety, it says Hongik University's Graduate School of Film, Digital Media & Communication began foundational research with the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency in March 2025, using 3D Gaussian Splatting in simulated crime-scene tests. MeTown is co-developing EVOVA Forensics with the university and has been running a proof of concept for crime-scene 3D profiling. The company says the system will go into live field testing on actual cases from August 2026, with the aim of integrating it into domestic forensic workflows within the year. It says it holds seven intellectual property assets, including certified test results, with related patent applications in progress.

The company lists a CES 2025 Innovation Award in fashion tech and 3D showrooms, selection for CES 2026, a Minister of Science and ICT commendation in July 2025, a TIPS program grant of KRW 500 million in November 2024, seed investment from JoyCity and CNT Tech in October 2024, the IBK Changong program in July 2025 and acceptance into the Korea Startup Center at Station F in Paris in December 2025. It also reports official collaboration with NVIDIA and Epic Games.

At the exhibition, working with Hongik University, MeTown says it aims to introduce EVOVA Forensics to domestic law enforcement and public safety agencies on the strength of its proof of concept with the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, and to test expansion into fire investigation, disaster response, insurance loss adjustment and facility safety inspection.

EVOVA Forensics has no export record yet, but the company says the EVOVA technology has international exposure: the CES awards, the Paris program and EVOVA 3D kiosks supplied to the Paris store of DANAYAD in France. It says overseas expansion will follow domestic law enforcement adoption in stages. The first target is the Southeast Asian police and public safety market, where it sees high demand for digital transformation and strong interest in Korean public safety technology, followed by the Middle East, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, where smart city projects are raising demand for public safety infrastructure. It is looking for public safety solution distributors that supply police and investigative agencies, and for system integrators in public safety and disaster response.

For plans, MeTown targets an official launch of EVOVA Forensics in October 2026, using the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency deployment as its first reference case. It will also submit the product for the CES 2027 Innovation Award. In the medium to long term it aims to expand beyond policing into fire investigation, disaster response, insurance loss adjustment, construction inspection and facility safety, growing into a spatial AI platform for community safety, with a business model of on-premise installed software and domain-specific extension packs, such as police analysis modules, on subscription.

The company names three difficulties. Government sales involve long decision cycles, complex procurement procedures and security certification requirements. The sensitivity of investigation data makes stable on-premise operation and data protection essential rather than cloud deployment, which is a significant burden for a 13-person startup. And it lacks channels to obtain security certifications and find local partners for overseas law enforcement markets. MeTown says help with public procurement participation, subsidies for security certification costs and buyer matching in the overseas public safety sector would be of real use.

t: COSMAS Bioscience Presents a Saliva-Based Drug Test Read by On-Device AI at KPEX 2026

blocks.cap: Photo - COSMAS Bioscience

blocks.x: A drug screening in the field depends on a person squinting at a test strip, and two people can read the same faint line differently. For a result that may be used in law enforcement, that variability is a weakness.

COSMAS Bioscience, Inc., a company in Gwanak-gu, Seoul, aims to eliminate the uncertainty of visual interpretation. Led by CEO Hojeong Yu, the company will take part in Korea Police World Expo 2026 (KPEX 2026), where it will show D-FREE, a field-deployable drug testing system that uses saliva.

COSMAS Bioscience, founded in 2024, says it specializes in high-sensitivity, rapid point-of-care diagnostic platforms and is currently focused on an integrated drug testing system for law enforcement and public safety. According to the company, its core technology combines a high-sensitivity saliva-based test kit, a compact portable optical reader and an on-device AI automated interpretation algorithm. The reader measures subtle optical signals from the kit and the AI analyzes and interprets them, which the company says overcomes the limits of visual interpretation, reduces differences between operators and makes results more objective and reliable.

D-FREE, the company says, uses a multiplex saliva kit that screens at the same time for five major drugs, including THC, methamphetamine, morphine, oxycodone and MDMA. It names four advantages: multiplex screening, AI-powered automated interpretation, high-sensitivity signal analysis and field usability. Because it pairs saliva testing with compact portable equipment, COSMAS says, D-FREE can be used quickly and conveniently in police enforcement and other public safety settings. The company says it aims to develop the system into a scalable on-site screening platform that can adapt quickly to emerging and novel drugs.

COSMAS says D-FREE is approaching commercialization and that it is carrying out validation to assess field applicability and commercial potential based on its core technologies and prototype development. In 2027, it plans to run field validation with the Korea National Police Agency to evaluate test performance, interpretation accuracy, user convenience and overall operability in real law enforcement settings. Based on the results, it intends to seek regulatory approval in Korea and the United States, through the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It also plans to show D-FREE at CES 2027 to reach international buyers and partners.

The company's goals at the exhibition are to introduce D-FREE to potential end users in law enforcement and public safety, gather feedback on their requirements and on real-world applicability, and find potential customers, distribution and business partners and strategic collaborators for its expansion into domestic and global public safety and drug screening markets.

COSMAS has no overseas sales yet, but it names the United States as its top-priority market and says it is preparing to enter. It points to a large U.S. market for drug screening and point-of-care diagnostics and strong demand for fast, accurate, portable field tests. After the United States, it plans to move into other major markets including Europe and China, and it expects demand for rapid and objective on-site drug screening to grow as illicit drug distribution and new psychoactive substances increase worldwide. The company is looking for local distributors of drug testing products, partners experienced in working with law enforcement agencies and organizations that can support regulatory approval and market entry, with the aim of building a framework that connects local validation, approval, distribution and business development.

Its plans are to strengthen D-FREE through further development and field validation with the Korea National Police Agency while preparing for approvals at home and abroad, to prioritize the United States for local validation and commercialization before Europe and China, and to work with local distributors and partners with experience in law enforcement agencies, pilot adoption and distribution networks. It also intends to use global exhibitions, such as CES 2027, to continue finding overseas buyers and to shape market-entry strategies for each country.

The company expects three difficulties: differences in regulatory and approval requirements for drug testing products between countries, securing opportunities for local field validation, and finding reliable distribution and business partners. It says country-specific regulatory consulting, connections with local public agencies and validation partners, buyer and distributor matching, participation in international exhibitions and follow-up business development support would help.

t: CNS Takes Autonomous Tower Crane Inspection Drones to FIX 2026

blocks.cap: Photo - CNS

blocks.x: Tower cranes, transmission lines and forests are hard for people to reach. They have long been inspected by workers who climb them or check them by eye, which carries the risk of falls, produces results that vary from person to person and leaves little record.

CNS Co., Ltd., an AI drone technology company based in Daedeok Innopolis, Daejeon, aims to replace that work with drones and AI. Led by CEO Junghyun Ahn, the company will exhibit at FIX 2026 and was named a winner in the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards. It will present DIMS (Drone Infrastructure Management System), an autonomous drone-based platform for inspecting and managing infrastructure.

CNS describes Ahn as a drone AI entrepreneur who builds drones that inspect tower cranes and infrastructure on their own, so workers no longer have to climb into danger. According to the company, DIMS brings the entire inspection workflow into one solution: drone flight, data capture, 3D digital twin creation, AI defect analysis and inspection history management. It says the system recognizes the shape of a target structure and generates its own flight path, and then recalculates the path in flight as the geometry changes or obstacles appear. AI detects defects such as cracks, corrosion, deformation and loose bolts, and marks where they are. CNS says all inspection records are stored on a cloud platform and compiled into reports automatically, so site teams and headquarters can share the same data in real time and asset owners can track changes over time.

The company names multi-sensor fusion (LiDAR, RGB, thermal, depth and inertial measurement unit sensors) and 3D reconstruction based on Visual SLAM and Gaussian Splatting as its core strengths. CNS says that by analyzing RGB, thermal and LiDAR data together, DIMS catches anomalies that are easy to miss by eye, and that inspectors can zoom into the mast, jib and joints of a crane from any angle without leaving the office. It describes DIMS as a hardware-agnostic software platform that works with a range of industrial drones and can be extended from tower cranes to transmission lines, forests and bridges.

CNS says its biggest differentiator is autonomous flight that understands structures whose shape keeps changing. Every tower crane is configured differently and changes height during construction, it explains, so conventional drone inspection that repeats a fixed route cannot keep up. The second is a platform that covers the full workflow, so customers do not have to piece together separate tools. The third is that DIMS is being validated on real Hyundai E&C construction sites rather than in a lab. The company names site safety managers and equipment managers at large construction companies as its primary users, followed by tower crane rental and maintenance companies, and later transmission line maintenance organizations and municipal wildfire monitoring teams.

CNS currently runs DIMS in three areas: tower crane inspection, transmission line inspection and wildfire monitoring. It reports cumulative revenue of USD 1.2 million with 171% annual growth, more than 120 field operations, 15,000 flights and a network of more than 50 partners. It has a corporate R&D center with 10 researchers, holds nine patents, and has carried out 12 government R&D projects backed by the Ministry of SMEs and Startups, the Ministry of Science and ICT, KOSMES and Daejeon Technopark. It is also a TIPS program company backed by Ansle Partners.

In Korea, the flagship project is with Hyundai E&C. CNS says it was selected for the 2026 Public-Private Open Innovation program with Hyundai E&C as the demand company, and is carrying out autonomous flights and building 3D digital twins of large tower cranes at a Hyundai E&C redevelopment site. It also works with GS E&C and supplies 3D digital twin data and AI training data to the software company Greneta. In the public sector, it was selected for the 2026 Public Demand-Based Problem-Solving Demonstration Program, where it is advancing fire and smoke detection AI, and it is running a drone-station-based wildfire monitoring pilot at Bomunsan in Daejeon. With Hanbat National University it is co-developing a SWIR-based LiDAR scanning module, and it works with KAIST on internships and research. It was also selected for the 2026 TIPS R&D program and for Daejeon Technopark's Growth Ladder (Post-BI) program.

Overseas, CNS says it is entering North America through Plug and Play and took part in the GMEP GOAL Program at its Sunnyvale headquarters in June 2026. It is pursuing a strategic partnership with the City of Detroit, gave a KOTRA investor relations (IR) presentation in Toronto and met MaRS and YSpace, and discussed cooperation with a local drone service company in Atlanta. In August 2026 it visited Bali and Jakarta, where it exhibited at JISMEX and held government and business meetings with state-owned PT Inti and PT Len, PT Anagile Kharisma Utama and APEKSI. It is also building a foothold in China, starting with an event in Shanghai, and says it is challenging for a CES 2027 Innovation Award. Its current export market is China. CNS wants to enter the U.S., describing North America as a market that can create high added value and the drone industry as a blue ocean. Finding buyers is its stated difficulty.

At the exhibition, CNS lists five aims. First, it will show results from the field: the 3D digital twins, AI defect detection results and inspection history dashboards built with Hyundai E&C, so visitors can follow the process from the drone planning its own flight path to the finished inspection report. Second, it wants to meet construction companies, project owners, public agencies and facility managers, and to look for partners in transmission line inspection and wildfire monitoring. Third, it will continue talks on local pilots, distribution and technical cooperation to speed entry into North America, Southeast Asia and China. Fourth, it will use feedback from visitors and experts to shape inspection items, report formats and operating methods. Fifth, it plans to raise awareness of the company and DIMS alongside a refreshed corporate identity and to broaden its network of investors and partners.

In Korea, CNS plans to make tower crane inspection a standard service based on the validation with construction companies, then extend DIMS to wildfire monitoring and transmission line inspection, including an unmanned wildfire monitoring system using drones and docking stations at Bomunsan. Over the medium to long term, it aims to supply DIMS overseas under a license model operated directly by local partners.

t: VISIONSPACE Takes Browser-Based Robot Layout Testing to FIX 2026

blocks.cap: Photo - VISIONSPACE

blocks.x: Layout, throughput, interference and collision problems often surface only after robots and automation equipment have been ordered. By then, fixing a layout means changing orders or reworking an installation.

VISIONSPACE Co., Ltd., a Physical AI simulation company based at the Startup Campus in Pangyo, says it addresses that problem by letting factory and logistics teams check layouts, robots and throughput in a browser before they buy. Led by CEO Wonseok Choi, the company will present its web-based platform, TESSERACT, to manufacturers, robot makers and media at FIX 2026, and it was recognized with an Innovation Award at the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards. It also says it hopes to find partners for overseas expansion at the show.

According to VISIONSPACE, TESSERACT runs on a standard PC without installation. It builds a 3D facility from a text prompt, a drawing or an image, simulates contact using mesh colliders based on actual shapes, and connects AI models to real robots through ROS2, TCP/IP and gRPC in both directions. The company says it provides predictions of key performance indicators (KPIs), overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) and return on investment (ROI) before introduction, and reports a measured sim-to-real behavioral error of less than 5%.

The company says Choi's background is in automotive manufacturing research and development, and describes him as someone who makes decisions on adopting equipment and robots, which once rested on drawings and experience, checkable as numbers in a browser. VISIONSPACE lists five points that set it apart. The first is a browser-based design that runs on an ordinary PC. The second is its own C++ engine with WebGPU, which does not depend on Unity, Unreal or Isaac Sim. The third is two registered Korean patents on robot model dataset generation and custom robot model generation. The fourth is the combination of real-shape mesh colliders with two-way ROS2, TCP/IP and gRPC control. The fifth is a loop that joins synthetic data generation with retraining on failure cases. The company adds that browser delivery alone is not the differentiator and that the strength lies in combining these elements.

It lists its target users as automation planning staff and factory and process engineers at manufacturing and logistics companies, distribution center operators, robot and material-handling equipment makers that want to add simulation to their quotations, automation consultants and system integrators, and public-sector facility digital twin managers. The main application areas are automotive and battery manufacturing, distribution centers, food logistics and public facilities.

VISIONSPACE reports several domestic projects. For Hyundai Movex, it built two real-time integrated control digital twins for an automated logistics center in Cheongna, Incheon, completed in April 2026. For LG Energy Solution and Mintech, it delivered a simulator for the automated process of recycling used EV batteries in February 2024. It has also carried out a warehouse simulation project for Samsung Welstory and built a sensor-based digital twin for the new digital headquarters of LX Korea Land and Geospatial Informatix Corporation. Projects covered by nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) are not named.

blocks.cap: Photo - VISIONSPACE

blocks.x: On the research side, the company is a co-research institution (2026 to 2028) in a national project led by the Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI) on AI-based open autonomous digital twin core technology, supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP). It is also running a deep-tech TIPS program project from the Ministry of SMEs and Startups on a real-time AI simulator for automated industrial robots (2024 to 2027). In a 2024 Gyeonggi Province metaverse industry convergence demonstration project, VISIONSPACE reports 100% accuracy in 3D asset generation against a 90% standard, 100% accuracy in remote control against a 99% standard over 10 trials, an average of 62.2 frames per second with 200 objects over 60 seconds, and a 720-hour process reproduced at 32 times speed in 22 hours. The company notes that these are results of that demonstration project.

Its awards include the top innovation technology award, the Daegu Mayor's Award, at the 2024 FIX Innovation Awards, and the Innovation Award at the 2026 FIX Innovation Awards. It also says it was selected for an excellent patent award in the first half of 2026 and received the top rating in performance evaluations of a startup-focused university program from 2024 to 2026. Its intellectual property includes two registered Korean patents (No. 10-2841574 and No. 10-2841575, registered July 29, 2025), 12 pending domestic applications and four U.S. applications.

The company is frank about its overseas position: it has not signed a direct export contract with an overseas company. It does list overseas work. In Saudi Arabia, it won a logistics digital twin and automated guided vehicle (AGV) operation simulation project for a new factory in the King Abdullah Economic City (KAEC) industrial area through the automation engineering affiliate of a large Korean company, which began in 2026. The contracting party is a Korean company, and the site where the work applies is in Saudi Arabia. In Japan, it signed a memorandum of understanding with OMRON in April 2024 and collaborated on a robot simulation proof of concept (PoC). In Germany, it is working with 123 Factory GmbH from June to November 2026 on a European market entry assessment and outreach under a Gangnam-gu overseas testbed program. In the U.S., it has taken part in the KSC Silicon Valley resident company program, the second-half U.S. program of KTOA's Venturium, and an English-language pitching event at K-AI Tech Week, and in September 2026 it visited NVIDIA's headquarters and met the person in charge of its Inception community. VISIONSPACE has also entered CES 2027 Innovation Awards and the 2027 Edison Awards, and says the results are not yet known.

Its preferred markets are the U.S., Germany and Europe, Japan, the Middle East including Saudi Arabia, and Taiwan, where it looks for robot and material-handling manufacturers, system integrators, automation consultants and channel partners. It names several difficulties: proving overseas references when contracts often pass through Korean prime contractors and NDAs, limited local sales networks, differing security and on-premise requirements, localization of materials, the cost of PoCs, and the expense of overseas events for a small team.

Its plan is to expand its subscription service in Korea and finish the KETI-led national project toward a logistics-focused software-as-a-service (SaaS) product. Overseas, it intends to expand step by step, from a Middle East reference and European PoCs to partnerships in the U.S. and Japan, with direct export contracts as the goal.

t: Deploying Hydrogen Refueling Stations Overseas Is Notoriously Complex — PLANTEC Wants to Change That With a Container-Sized Package

blocks.cap: PLANTEC staff inspect the H2 PRG System’s hydrogen refueling module | Photo - PLANTEC

blocks.x: A hydrogen refueling station is not a single piece of equipment. It is a compressor, a storage system, a dispenser, pressurized piping, and an entire layer of electrical, control, and safety systems that all have to work together on one site. Building one is complicated enough at home. Overseas, where design codes, equipment procurement, construction practices, and installation conditions differ from country to country and even project to project, sourcing and assembling those systems piece by piece can turn a single infrastructure project into a long list of local unknowns.
What if the core of a hydrogen station could be built once, tested at the factory, and shipped out as a single package instead of assembled from scratch on-site?

PLANTEC Co., Ltd., a Korea-based engineering company founded in 1982, is answering that question. The company built its business on steel-plant EPC (engineering, procurement, fabrication and construction) work and has spent more than four decades extending that experience into industrial equipment, environmental facilities, and energy infrastructure projects, backed by a domestic fabrication base that covers everything from design to equipment manufacturing, installation, and construction. PLANTEC is now applying that track record to the H2 PRG System, a modular hydrogen energy platform, and its refueling component, the R Module, which the company has already built as a working prototype.

H2 PRG stands for Production, Refueling, and Generation — the three stages of the hydrogen value chain the system connects within one architecture. Each function is configured as an independent module and linked through standardized hydrogen, power, and control interfaces, so a customer can install only the functions a given project needs and expand later without redesigning the whole system. The Production stage, or P Module, is designed to connect with a project's own hydrogen source — including water electrolysis — to supply hydrogen on site, while the Generation stage, or G Module, is designed to route surplus hydrogen into fuel cells for distributed power, EV charging, or external electricity supply. PLANTEC is also pursuing commercialization of additional clean-hydrogen technologies, including water electrolysis and hydrogen purification, to widen the production options the platform can eventually draw on.

The R Module, the refueling piece of that platform, has moved past the concept stage: it is designed for approximately 50 kg/h of hydrogen refueling capacity and 70 MPa (10,000 psi) dispensing pressure, integrating compressors, storage systems, dispensers, piping, and control and safety systems into a single container-type package built for transport and on-site installation. PLANTEC says the packaged R Module reduces required site area by approximately 17%, building area by approximately 39%, and estimated deployment time by approximately 25% compared with a conventional hydrogen refueling station. Gas and flame detection, automatically actuated valves, and a combination of natural and forced ventilation are built into the design to respond to abnormal hydrogen conditions.
According to PLANTEC, the R Module was developed specifically to reduce the complexity of sourcing and installing hydrogen refueling equipment locally, project by project.

blocks.cap: PLANTEC’s container-type H2 PRG System installed at an industrial site | Photo - PLANTEC

blocks.x: PLANTEC is featuring the H2 PRG System and the R Module in the CES 2027 Innovation Awards program, treating the submission as a launch point for introducing the platform to buyers outside Korea before it has an overseas commercial project on the books. PLANTEC says the CES showing marks the starting point for turning its domestic hydrogen-plant construction experience into a transportable, modular product it can introduce to a global audience.

PLANTEC frames the innovation in H2 PRG less as a new piece of hydrogen hardware than as an integration layer: rather than developing its own electrolyzer, dispenser, or fuel cell, the company says its value lies in connecting hydrogen technologies that already exist through a shared hydrogen backbone, standardized interfaces, and an integrated control architecture, so hydrogen produced on site can be routed either to mobility use or, through a fuel cell, converted into power as demand shifts. PLANTEC calls modularity and scalability the platform's biggest advantage: a customer can install only the functions a project needs today and add production, storage, refueling, or generation capacity later without redesigning the system from the ground up, because major equipment is factory-packaged and pre-tested before it reaches the site and then connected there through the same standardized interfaces. PLANTEC says that approach is meant to make hydrogen infrastructure easier to repeat across different locations rather than engineered from zero each time.

The R Module builds on hydrogen experience PLANTEC has already put into operation. The company has completed a steam methane reforming (SMR)-based LNG reforming facility with a hydrogen production capacity of 360 Nm³/h, and it is currently building an autothermal reforming (ATR)-based hydrogen production facility for POSCO's HyREX hydrogen-reduced ironmaking project, designed for roughly 34,000 Nm³/h, or about 25,000 tons of hydrogen a year. PLANTEC has also carried out a hydrogen pipeline network project in Pohang and, together with group affiliate MiCoPower, is building a 2.85 MW fuel-cell power plant. In its CES 2027 Innovation Awards submission, PLANTEC presents the R Module as the physical refueling module of the H2 PRG System — the one piece of the platform it has already turned from concept into hardware.

blocks.cap: Rendering of PLANTEC’s modular H2 PRG System for hydrogen production, refueling and generation | Photo - PLANTEC

blocks.x: PLANTEC does not yet have a commercial export contract or an overseas project for H2 PRG, and the company is direct about what stands between the prototype and that point. Hydrogen refueling stations have to satisfy codes covering high-pressure gas systems, pressure vessels, explosion protection, electrical systems, fire safety, and controls, and these vary by country — meaning the same R Module could need design or equipment changes depending on where it is deployed, and PLANTEC expects to work with local engineering and certification specialists as it moves into specific markets. The company also says overseas customers are asking for operating history, not just specifications, before they commit — proof of safety, performance, and maintenance under real conditions. PLANTEC is now looking for demonstration sites, in Korea and abroad, and plans to use the operating data it gathers there to build confidence with future customers overseas.

blocks.cap: PLANTEC’s H2 PRG System deployed at Kangrim Heavy Industries’ Pohang facility | Photo - PLANTEC

blocks.x: For international expansion, PLANTEC is prioritizing the United States, where it points to demand tied to renewable energy, distributed power, hydrogen mobility, and industrial hydrogen infrastructure, with potential applications at logistics hubs, ports, airports, industrial sites, and other locations that could use a modular, scalable refueling system. The company plans to use CES 2027 to connect with U.S. customers, energy companies, project developers, and technology partners. blocks.cap: Concept image showing the H2 PRG System linking hydrogen production, refueling, storage and power generation | Photo - PLANTEC

blocks.x: Looking ahead, PLANTEC's first priority is securing an operating record for the R Module and verifying its performance and safety before converting that into commercial projects and product sales, both in Korea and abroad. Beyond the R Module, the company plans to expand integration of the P Module for hydrogen production and the G Module for fuel-cell power generation as it builds out the rest of the H2 PRG platform, refining the R Module's design along the way to meet country-specific codes and certification requirements. Rather than making large upfront investments in its own overseas facilities, PLANTEC says it intends to grow abroad through demand-driven projects, commercial sales, and partnerships with local companies, combining its hydrogen-plant EPC track record with its modular product line.

t: ﻿MilliTrack Targets Dust- and Steam-Filled Factories With an RF Localization Add-On for AMRs

blocks.cap: MilliTrack AMR Plus Tracker and Tag, an RF-based localization solution for autonomous mobile robots | Photo - MilliTrack

blocks.x: Autonomous mobile robots are becoming more common across factories, yet most still rely heavily on LiDAR and cameras to determine their position on the floor. These systems can lose track of a robot's location in dust, steam, or smoke, limiting automation in industries such as steel, chemicals, and food processing. In the global steel industry, 36% of accidents occur under low-visibility conditions, and in the United Kingdom's food and drink industry, such conditions account for 25% of casualties.
If a robot could keep its bearings even when it cannot see, plants in these industries could automate operations that still depend on workers moving through hazardous, low-visibility areas today.

blocks.cap: MilliTrack AMR Plus Tracker provides 3 cm localization accuracy at distances of up to 30 meters and supports multiple industrial interfaces | Photo - MilliTrack

blocks.x: MilliTrack Co., Ltd., a spin-off from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), is addressing that gap with AMR+, a radio frequency (RF) localization add-on that helps autonomous mobile robots maintain positioning accuracy in low-visibility industrial environments. The system is installed in two parts: an AMR+ Tracker mounted on the robot, and AMR+ Tags placed only in the specific low-visibility zones where the AMR's optical sensors fail, with no network or power cabling required. According to MilliTrack, installation takes only minutes, and AMR+ integrates with an AMR's existing localization stack, leaving current workflows largely unchanged.

MilliTrack says AMR+ addresses that gap with its patented millimeter-wave technology, protected by 22 patents, which delivers 3 cm localization accuracy over a 30 m range even in environments dense with metal structures and machinery — a level of precision the company describes as the best among RF localization products on the market. AMR+ also provides collision avoidance that meets the IEC TS61496-5 safety standard.

blocks.cap: MilliTrack AMR Plus Tag requires no network or power cabling and offers up to 20 years of battery life | Photo - MilliTrack

blocks.x: MilliTrack was founded by CEO Songmin Kim, a KAIST professor with more than 15 years of experience in mobile sensing research, as a university spin-off. The company's core localization technology has won 11 awards, including multiple Best Paper Awards at the Association for Computing Machinery's MobiSys conference. According to MilliTrack, its localization system is already deployed at multiple global enterprises in heavy industry and manufacturing, with more than 30 ongoing proof-of-concept projects spanning robotics, automotive and smart factory applications.

Beyond safety, MilliTrack highlights the operational costs of losing localization. Remapping an AMR fleet after a facility layout change can take up to an hour, at an average loss of USD 260,000 per instance, according to the company. Because Tag-based localization is unaffected by drift or layout changes, MilliTrack says AMR+ removes much of that remapping overhead. AMR+ Tags require no network or power cabling and run up to 20 years on a single battery, according to the company. The company is targeting plant operators in heavy industries, chemicals and food processing, along with the broader dust- and steam-exposed manufacturing sectors — including chemicals, food and beverage, petroleum and coal, and wood — that together account for nearly 50% of U.S. manufacturing.

blocks.cap: MilliTrack AMR Plus deployment process, from mounting the tracker and installing tags to automatic configuration and operation | Photo - MilliTrack

blocks.x: MilliTrack is positioning AMR+ as a retrofit option for plant operators looking to expand automation without replacing their existing AMR fleets, and says it is seeking partnerships with AMR manufacturers, robotics system integrators and industrial automation providers as it expands into global manufacturing and logistics markets. The company projects that AMR+ could reach more than 200,000 units in adoption and USD 1.5 billion in revenue, citing the size of the dust- and steam-exposed manufacturing market as its addressable opportunity — figures MilliTrack presents as its own outlook rather than independently verified market data.

MilliTrack submitted AMR+ for the CES 2027 Innovation Awards in the Construction & Industrial Tech, Embedded Technologies, Robotics, and Supply & Logistics categories, and the company will exhibit at CES 2027 with a dedicated booth.

t: Launch Vehicles Opened the Space Industry and Satellites Expanded It — the Rover Is Next...

blocks.cap: Provided by Unmanned Exploration Laboratory (UEL)

blocks.x: On a lunar surface covered in extreme cold, extreme heat and dust, Unmanned Exploration Laboratory took on the challenge by developing its rover technologies in-house.
With lunar delivery costing 1.2 million USD per kilogram, the lighter Scarab lowers the cost barrier to lunar exploration.

The space industry has expanded step by step as new modes of transportation have been added. Launch vehicles opened the path beyond Earth, and the satellites that followed created a new market in communications and observation. The next stage is the rover. While a lander can only observe the area immediately around its landing site, a rover — depending on its specifications — can travel from a few hundred meters to several kilometers on its own to survey the moon's terrain and resources. Building on this shift from a lander's "eyes" to a rover's "feet," Unmanned Exploration Laboratory Co., Ltd. (UEL; CEO Jaeho Lee) is taking on the CES 2027 Innovation Awards with its micro lunar exploration rover, Scarab.

UEL's story goes back to 2017, when it was selected as a family company under the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI)'s STAR-Exploration project — a program in which KARI selects and supports promising companies with space exploration technology. UEL was formally incorporated in 2023 and has focused solely on developing lunar exploration rovers ever since, without diversifying into other businesses.

blocks.cap: Provided by Unmanned Exploration Laboratory (UEL)

blocks.x: The challenge was that the lunar surface follows none of Earth's rules. Day-to-night temperatures swing between extreme cold and extreme heat, fine vibration and radiation threaten electronic equipment, and finely ground dust works its way into every gap and wears down mechanical parts. UEL took on each of these extreme conditions and built up its rover technologies in-house, securing core technologies across the body and battery, data transmission and reception, imaging, and the electronic speed controller (ESC). The company has also expanded its business model from rover manufacturing and parts supply to payload services and image-data sales, and envisions eventually becoming the mode of transportation for an "Earth-Moon economy" that extends all the way to resource recovery.

Scarab, which is taking the stage at CES, is a two-wheel rover with a total weight of 2 kg and dimensions of 254 (W) × 285 (D) × 194 (H) mm. Its body is made of Al 6061-T6 alloy, making it both lightweight and sturdy. Even while carrying two cameras, it can accommodate about 300 g of payload, and it is being prepared for deployment on lunar exploration missions planned for 2027 and 2028.

Scarab's biggest advantage is its light weight itself. Based on publicly disclosed pricing for commercial lunar delivery services, sending 1 kg to the lunar surface costs roughly 1.2 million USD on a per-lander basis — meaning mission costs rise in step with a rover's weight. UEL turned this cost structure on its head: by cutting the rover's weight to 2 kg, it can significantly lower the cost burden of a mission while also making use of a large lander's spare payload capacity, which lowers the barrier to adoption for lander operators as well. Scarab is also designed with a top-bottom symmetric structure so that it can drive regardless of which side it lands on after being dropped, and its hemispherical mesh-grouser wheels and circular tail are designed to absorb and disperse landing impact.

The onboard computer (OBC) that serves as the rover's "brain" is also worth a closer look. It integrates control of the camera, IMU, motor, communications, and power systems, supports CAN, RS-422, and RS-485 interfaces, and applies a modular design built on a low-power, high-reliability architecture based on conduction cooling. When multiple Scarab units operate together, the OBC also serves as a communication relay linking rovers in shadowed or obstructed terrain with the lander. This OBC has already been proven in the field: it completed on-orbit verification aboard the COSMIC CubeSat (3U) on the Nuri rocket's fourth launch in November 2025, and will undergo further verification aboard UEL's own satellite, UEL-Y-Sys (6U), on the upcoming fifth launch scheduled for Oct. 7. On the ground, it has also completed thermal-vacuum testing (10⁻⁵ torr, -40°C to +100°C), drop-impact testing, driving tests on an artificial lunar-regolith testbed, and structural and vibration analysis.

blocks.cap: Provided by Unmanned Exploration Laboratory (UEL)

blocks.x: UEL holds more than 14 registered patents and has published more than 60 domestic and international academic papers, and has carried out technology transfers with KARI, the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute (KERI), and others. Overseas, the company is finalizing payload plans with multiple global space companies participating in NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, aiming to place its rovers in the spare capacity aboard their landers. UEL is pursuing a 2027 mission with some of these operators and a 2028 mission with a Japanese commercial lunar lander operator. In Korea, the company is co-developing a folding-wheel rover with KAIST, and is a co-organizing and sponsoring partner of the Korea Space Rover Challenge together with the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, and Sacheon City.

UEL's reasons for pursuing the CES 2027 Innovation Awards come down to three: expanding global cooperation and securing an early market position, having its technology objectively assessed by outside experts through CES judging, and converting a track record that has so far been recognized only within Korea into internationally certified results. Because a proven track record is what determines mission adoption in the space industry, UEL's goal is to get onto an overseas mission early and establish itself as the "first verified micro lunar exploration rover." Starting in 2027, UEL plans to use the funding it secures toward lander payload costs, carrying out a mission demonstration every year, while also expanding its payload and data business by supplying the lunar-surface image data Scarab collects to client companies.

UEL is preparing for this challenge with support from from KimVenturous CEO Hyunsung Kim, a consulting firm that advises companies competing for the CES Innovation Awards on their participation strategy. KimVenturous helps Korean startups enter CES with its know-how in winning CES Innovation Awards and its strategic consulting, and is supporting companies preparing for CES together with AVING News. Over the past 22 years, AVING News has partnered with more than 800 media outlets across 54 countries to introduce Korean companies to the world, and in August 2025 it launched the International Press Club to support Korean companies' global expansion.
